title: Neural Networks in Trading: Decomposition Instead of Scaling — Building Modules
text:
Introduction
In
the previous article
, we began working on implementing our own vision of the approaches proposed by the authors of the
SSCNN
framework. In this article, we will continue by moving on to the practical aspects of implementing the framework's key components. However, before delving into the code and algorithms, it is important to remind the reader of the strengths of
SSCNN
and how it works. Understanding these fundamentals will allow you not only to replicate the implementation but also to consciously adapt it to real-world trading tasks.
The
SSCNN
(
Segmental Structured Convolutional Neural Network
) framework was developed as a specialized tool for analyzing time series under conditions of market instability and fragmented signals. Its central idea is to process not individual values, but complete data segments, allowing the model to take into account both local features and broader contextual dependencies. Instead of a linear view of a time series,
SSCNN
offers a stratified approach: each time interval is considered within the structure of its surrounding context, making it possible to accurately extract meaningful features even in the presence of a high level of noise.
In the first stage, the data undergo a structural decomposition process, in which the signal is broken down into stable components: a long-term trend, seasonal variations, short-term fluctuations, and residual noise. This step is particularly important when working with financial time series, where trends and short-term deviations carry different analytical significance. Separate processing models are created for each component, which improves the quality of the analysis and the interpretability of the results. The final forecast is built as a coherent aggregation of outputs from these models.
In
SSCNN
, particular emphasis is placed on the
attention-based normalization mechanism (
AttnNorm
). This component not only stabilizes the model's internal representations but also allows it to adaptively focus on the most informative parts of the data. In conditions of market turbulence, where the signal can be significantly distorted by short-term spikes, this selectivity ensures the stability and accuracy of the forecast. Normalization is implemented with the segmental context taken into account and includes the training of attention parameters, making backpropagation more meaningful and targeted.
An author-created visualization of the
SSCNN
framework is shown below.
Component Extraction Module
In the practical section of the previous article, we focused on implementing a normalization kernel with attention weights in the
OpenCL
environment. This work allowed us to lay the groundwork for the fast, parallel execution of key operations: calculating mean values and standard deviations across data segments while accounting for attention weights, as well as directly normalizing the input signal. All of this is performed within the
GPU
context, which ensures high performance and scalability of the solution.
Today, we are naturally continuing the work we started earlier and shifting our focus to how the main program interacts with these
OpenCL
kernels. We need to implement the algorithms for handling them, including buffer preparation, configuration of call parameters, synchronization, and verification of the integrity of the transmitted data. This is an important step: after all, the effectiveness of the
SSCNN
framework depends largely not only on the mathematical accuracy of the kernel, but also on how competently and coherently data exchange between the CPU and the GPU is organized.
The central element of the design is the
CNeuronAttentNorm
object. It is responsible for coordinating the interaction between the high-level logic of the attention normalization layer and low-level
GPU
computation. This object inherits from the base class
CNeuronBaseOCL
, which provides it with a universal interface and allows it to be integrated into the overall model stack without losing flexibility. The structure of the new object is shown below.
class
CNeuronAttentNorm :
public
CNeuronBaseOCL
  {
protected
:
uint
iPeriod;
uint
iVariables;
uint
iCount;
//---
CParams                 cAttention;
   CNeuronSoftMaxOCL       cSoftMax;
   CNeuronBaseOCL          cMeans;
   CNeuronBaseOCL          cSTDevs;
//---
virtual

AttentNorm(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL);
virtual
bool
AttentNormGrad(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL);
//---
virtual
bool
feedForward(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
override
;
virtual
bool
updateInputWeights(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
override
;
virtual
bool
calcInputGradients(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
override
;
public
:
                     CNeuronAttentNorm(
void
) :  iPeriod(
0
), iVariables(
0
), iCount(
0
) {};
                    ~CNeuronAttentNorm(
void
) {};
//---
virtual
bool

numOutputs,
uint
myIndex, COpenCLMy *open_cl,
uint
units_count,
uint
period,

variables,
                          ENUM_OPTIMIZATION optimization_type,

batch);
//---
virtual
bool

const
int
file_handle)
override
;

bool

const
int

)

const
{
return

virtual
void

override
;
//---
CNeuronBaseOCL*   GetMeans(
void
) {
return
cMeans.AsObject(); }
   CNeuronBaseOCL*   GetSTDevs(
void
) {
return
cSTDevs.AsObject(); }
virtual
uint
GetPeriod(
void
)
const
{
return
iPeriod; }

uint
GetVariables(

void
)

{

//---

bool

In the class structure, we can see that the key internal parameters are
iPeriod
,
iVariables
, and
iCount
: they specify the size of the data segment, the number of variables, and the number of segments in a single unit sequence, respectively. These values define the structure of the array being analyzed.
Special attention should be paid to the
cAttention
object, which stores parameters related to the attention mechanism, and to
cSoftMax
: the component that converts attention weights into a normalized form. These two modules work in close coordination: the trainable attention parameters undergo a
SoftMax
transformation, and only then are they used to compute the means and standard deviations. The
cMeans
and
cSTDevs
objects are used to store these statistics.
All internal objects of the
CNeuronAttentNorm
class are declared statically,class are allocated as embedded members, which makes their lifecycle predictable
.
This approach allows us to leave both the constructor and the destructor empty. The allocation and release of resources are delegated to explicit management within the model's lifecycle. The main initialization of all internal and inherited components occurs centrally in the
Init
method, which accepts runtime environment and layer configuration parameters.
bool
CNeuronAttentNorm::Init(
uint
numOutputs,
uint
myIndex, COpenCLMy *open_cl,
uint
units_count,
uint
period,
uint
variables,
                             ENUM_OPTIMIZATION optimization_type,
uint
batch)
  {
if
(!CNeuronBaseOCL::Init(numOutputs, myIndex, open_cl, units_count * period * variables,
                                                                 optimization_type, batch))
return
false
;
   CNeuronBaseOCL::SetActivationFunction(None);
First, control is passed to the method of the same name in the parent class, where all inherited interfaces are already initialized. We then explicitly set the activation function type to
None
, since this layer does not perform any nonlinear transformations on its own — its entire task is focused on normalization using attention weights.
Next, we save the layer configuration parameters: the number of blocks (
units
), the number of variables, and the segmentation period. These values will later be used to control the internal normalization logic.
iCount = units_count;
   iVariables = variables;
   iPeriod = period;
We then proceed to initialize the newly declared objects. The first is the
cAttention
object, which is responsible for generating attention weights. After successful initialization, we disable the activation function, leaving the result in linear form.
if
(!cAttention.Init(
0
,
0
, OpenCL, iPeriod * iVariables, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cAttention.SetActivationFunction(None);
if
(!cSoftMax.Init(
0
,
1
, OpenCL, cAttention.Neurons(), optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cSoftMax.SetHeads(iVariables);
Next, the
cSoftMax
component is configured to convert the attention values into a probability distribution. Its dimension corresponds to the number of neurons in
cAttention
. The
SetHeads
method specifies the number of
attention heads
— here, it is set equal to the number of variables, which allows each feature to be processed independently.
Next, a
cMeans
object is created, which will be used to store the mean values for the segments. The dimensionality is determined by the number of blocks multiplied by the number of variables. The activation function is disabled again, since this is a statistical characteristic.
//---
if
(!cMeans.Init(
0
,
2
, OpenCL, iCount * iVariables, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cMeans.SetActivationFunction(None);
if
(!cSTDevs.Init(
0
,
3
, OpenCL, iCount * iVariables, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cSTDevs.SetActivationFunction(None);
//---
return
true
;
  }
The
cSTDevs
block, which stores the standard deviation values required for normalization, is configured in a similar manner. It uses exactly the same configuration as
cMeans
.
Thus, the
Init
method establishes a robust architectural foundation for the
CNeuronAttentNorm
layer by integrating logical and computational components into a single, easily scalable system. Each object is responsible for a well-defined stage of processing, and centralized initialization provides full control over the layer parameters and behavior in the
OpenCL
context.
Once all internal components have been initialized, the key step is to organize the forward pass through the layer. It is at this stage that the model begins to use the previously initialized structures (attention weights, the
SoftMax
transformation, and objects for statistical characteristics) to perform its main task: normalizing the input data while taking into account the importance of each element. The algorithm is implemented in the
feedForward
method.
bool
CNeuronAttentNorm::feedForward(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
if
(bTrain)
     {
if
(!cAttention.FeedForward())
return
false
;
if
(!cSoftMax.FeedForward(cAttention.AsObject()))
return
false
;
     }
//---
return
AttentNorm(NeuronOCL);
  }
The method takes as an argument a pointer to a
NeuronOCL
object that represents the preceding neural layer containing the data being analyzed.
If the model is in training mode (
bTrain == true
), the first step is to perform a forward pass through the
cAttention
component, where
raw attention values
are computed. These values do not directly depend on the current state of the input data and are generated during the model training process. Consequently, during operation, the block's outputs will be unchanged, and there is no need to perform unnecessary operations on every pass.
The attention coefficients are then passed to the
cSoftMax
block, which converts them into a normalized probability distribution. This step is critically important: it ensures that the sum of the attention weights across the segment equals one, thereby ensuring the correctness of subsequent calculations.
Regardless of the current mode (whether it is training or inference), the final step of the
feedForward
method is to call the
AttentNorm
function. This function acts as a wrapper around the
OpenCL
kernel of the same name and handles all low-level preparation: from setting parameters to queuing the task for execution. The method's structure strictly follows the standard pattern adopted for all such calls, and this standardization becomes particularly evident thanks to the previously implemented macros and generic patterns. In light of this, we will deliberately refrain from delving into the internal implementation of
AttentNorm
in detail, limiting ourselves to recognizing it as a standard and technically correct point of integration between the model logic and the
OpenCL
context.
Once the forward pass is complete, an equally important step follows: calculating the error gradients needed to correctly update the model's weights. This process is implemented in the
calcInputGradients
method and follows a clear backpropagation logic.
bool
CNeuronAttentNorm::calcInputGradients(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
if
(!AttentNormGrad(NeuronOCL))
return
false
;
if
(NeuronOCL.Activation() != None)
if
(!DeActivation(NeuronOCL.getOutput(), NeuronOCL.getGradient(),
                       NeuronOCL.getGradient(), NeuronOCL.Activation()))
return
false
;
The method begins with a call to
AttentNormGrad
, which, by analogy with
AttentNorm
, serves as an interface to the
OpenCL
kernel of the same name. Its task is to collect the gradients from the normalized output signal, taking into account the attention characteristics and the parameters of the current data segment. This is a crucial step, since it provides the basis for accounting, in reverse, for the influence of the input data on the final statistics, such as the mean and variance.
Next, a check is performed: if an activation function was specified for the input layer, the obtained gradients must be differentiated with the specified nonlinearity taken into account. This is implemented by calling the
DeActivation
function, which adjusts the gradients, thereby ensuring full compliance with the classic backward pass scheme.
The final step of the method is to propagate the gradients back along the attention chain. To do this, the
CalcHiddenGradients
method of the
cAttention
object is used; the output gradient from the
SoftMax
module is passed to it as input. This procedure ensures a continuous flow of gradient information from the output layer to the model's hidden parameters and, ultimately, to its inputs.
if
(!cAttention.CalcHiddenGradients(cSoftMax.AsObject()))
return
false
;
//---
return
true
;
  }
The process of updating the parameters in the attention normalization module is completed by the
updateInputWeights
method, which is responsible for adjusting the internal weights based on the accumulated gradients. In this case, the method implementation is extremely concise: control is passed to the function of the same name in the
cAttention
object, which is responsible for generating attention coefficients. This is fully consistent with the overall architecture of the
SSCNN
framework, in which each component of the model is responsible for its own portion of the computations.
bool
CNeuronAttentNorm::updateInputWeights(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
return
cAttention.UpdateInputWeights();
  }
This approach ensures a high degree of modularity and flexibility in the system: the attention mechanism is encapsulated in its own object, which simplifies both debugging and the subsequent adaptation of the model to new conditions. In addition, direct delegation of control makes the code cleaner and easier to read, and also facilitates the reuse of components without having to rewrite them.
This concludes our discussion of the normalization layer methods that take attention coefficients into account. We traced the entire logical sequence — from the initialization of internal objects to the final stages of the forward and backward passes, including gradient distribution and weight updates. We would like to emphasize that all key computations and control operations are performed within a single coherent interface.
The complete source code for the
CNeuronAttentNorm
class and all of its methods is provided in the attachment.
Extraction of the Spatial Component
Moving on to the next logical block of the architecture, let us examine an object designed to extract the spatial component during attention-based normalization. We are referring to the
CNeuronSAttentNorm
class, which extends the functionality of
CNeuronTransposeOCL
and, unlike the previous implementation, is designed to process transposed data, providing additional flexibility when working with spatial and contextually distributed features.
class
CNeuronSAttentNorm :
public
CNeuronTransposeOCL
  {
protected
:
   CNeuronTransposeOCL     cTranspose;
   CNeuronBaseOCL          cAttention;
   CNeuronSoftMaxOCL       cSoftMax;
   CNeuronBaseOCL          cMeans;
   CNeuronBaseOCL          cSTDevs;
   CNeuronBaseOCL          cNorm;
//---
virtual
bool
AttentNorm(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL);
virtual
bool
AttentNormGrad(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL);
//---
virtual
bool
feedForward(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
override
;
virtual
bool
calcInputGradients(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
override
;
public
:
                     CNeuronSAttentNorm(
void
) {};
                    ~CNeuronSAttentNorm(
void
) {};
//---
virtual
bool
Init(
uint
numOutputs,
uint
myIndex, COpenCLMy *open_cl,
uint
units_count,
uint
variables,
                          ENUM_OPTIMIZATION optimization_type,
uint
batch);
//---
virtual
bool
Load(
const
int
file_handle)
override
;
//---
virtual
int
Type(
void
)
override
const
{
return
defNeuronSAttentNorm; }
virtual
void
SetOpenCL(COpenCLMy *obj)
override
;
//---
CNeuronBaseOCL*   GetMeans(
void
) {
return
cMeans.AsObject(); }
   CNeuronBaseOCL*   GetSTDevs(
void
) {
return
cSTDevs.AsObject(); }
virtual
uint
GetVariables(
void
)
const
{
return
iWindow; }
virtual
uint
GetUnits(
void
)
const
{
return
iCount; }
//---
virtual
void
SetActivationFunction(ENUM_ACTIVATION value)
override
{  activation = None; }
  };
The structure of this object is essentially a mirror image of the
CNeuronAttentNorm
layer discussed earlier, but with a key difference in how the attention coefficients are generated. The normalization itself is performed along the feature axis within the window.
As before, initialization of the
CNeuronSAttentNorm
object is handled in the
Init
method of the same name, which is responsible for correctly configuring all of the layer’s internal components and preparing them to perform the forward and backward passes.
bool
CNeuronSAttentNorm::Init(
uint
numOutputs,
uint
myIndex, COpenCLMy *open_cl,
uint
units_count,
uint
variables,
                              ENUM_OPTIMIZATION optimization_type,
uint
batch)
  {
if
(!CNeuronTransposeOCL::Init(numOutputs, myIndex, open_cl, units_count, variables,
                                                            optimization_type, batch))
return
false
;
   activation = None;
First, the method of the same name in the parent class
CNeuronTransposeOCL
is called, providing the basic configuration of the current layer's parameters, including inherited interfaces. After that, the layer's activation function is explicitly set to
None
, since activation is not applied at this stage.
Next, the sequential initialization of all internal objects begins, each of which plays a specific role in the computational process. The
cTranspose
object is responsible for transposing the input tensor, converting the temporal slice into a feature vector that the attention module will subsequently process.
if
(!cTranspose.Init(
0
,
0
, OpenCL, iWindow, iCount, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
Next, a
cAttention
object is created and configured; in this case, it serves solely as a buffer for storing attention coefficients.
if
(!cAttention.Init(
0
,
1
, OpenCL, iWindow * iWindow, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cAttention.SetActivationFunction(None);
if
(!cSoftMax.Init(
0
,
2
, OpenCL, cAttention.Neurons(), optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cSoftMax.SetHeads(iWindow);
This is followed by the associated cSoftMax block, which normalizes the weights along a specified dimension — in this case, the feature dimension.
Next, the mean-value object
cMeans
and the standard-deviation object
cSTDevs
are initialized; these are required for the subsequent scaling and alignment of the data being analyzed.
if
(!cMeans.Init(
0
,
3
, OpenCL, iCount, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cMeans.SetActivationFunction(None);
if
(!cSTDevs.Init(
0
,
4
, OpenCL, iCount, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cSTDevs.SetActivationFunction(None);
The configuration is completed by the
cNorm
object, which is a buffer that stores normalized data before it is transposed back into a time-series representation.
if
(!cNorm.Init(
0
,
5
, OpenCL, Neurons(), optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cNorm.SetActivationFunction(None);
//---
return
true
;
  }
Once initialization is complete, the
CNeuronSAttentNorm
object becomes fully functional, and we can move on to examining the key stage — the forward pass. This method plays a central role in processing the data being analyzed, transforming it step by step using the layer's internal computational blocks.
bool
CNeuronSAttentNorm::feedForward(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
if
(!cTranspose.FeedForward(NeuronOCL))
return
false
;
The forward pass begins by calling the
FeedForward
method of the
cTranspose
object, which is responsible for the initial transformation of the input tensor. At this stage, the data is reorganized so that the time window is unfolded into a spatial representation. This is necessary for further work with the attention matrix, in which each feature will be compared with all the others.
The next step is to call the
MatMul
function, which performs matrix multiplication of the input data by its transposed copy. This creates an attention matrix, where each row contains attention scores reflecting the relevance of the other elements to the current feature. The result of this operation is stored in the
cAttention
object, which represents a raw, as-yet-unnormalized attention map.
if
(!MatMul(NeuronOCL.getOutput(), cTranspose.getOutput(), cAttention.getOutput(),
              iWindow, iCount, iWindow,
1
,
false
))
return
false
;
if
(!cSoftMax.FeedForward(cAttention.AsObject()))
return
false
;
Once the attention matrix has been obtained, it must be normalized. To do this, the
FeedForward
method of the
cSoftMax
object is called; this converts numerical values into probabilistic weights, thereby ensuring the interpretability and numerical stability of subsequent calculations.
The resulting attention weights are then passed to the
AttentNorm
method, which implements the core idea of the layer: scaling and normalizing the input data based on the calculated attention coefficients. This stage combines the statistical characteristics of the window (mean and standard deviation) while taking into account the importance of each feature, allowing the model to identify structural patterns in the data even in the presence of significant noise or biases.
if
(!AttentNorm(cTranspose.AsObject()))
return
false
;
//---
return
CNeuronTransposeOCL::feedForward(cNorm.AsObject());
  }
The final step is to pass control to the
feedForward
method of the base class
CNeuronTransposeOCL
, where the normalized data tensor
cNorm
is processed. This returns the obtained results to the input-data representation.
Now that we have finished discussing the forward pass, it makes sense to move on to an equally important step — backpropagation. The
calcInputGradients
method is responsible for calculating the gradients needed to subsequently adjust the model's weights and parameters during training. Here, a step-by-step sequence of operations is implemented to return the error signal from the model's output layer to its input, taking into account all internal transformations, including the attention mechanism and normalization.
bool
CNeuronSAttentNorm::calcInputGradients(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
if
(!NeuronOCL)
return
false
;
//---
if
(!CNeuronTransposeOCL::calcInputGradients(cNorm.AsObject()))
return
false
;
The procedure begins with a basic validity check of the pointer to the input data object
NeuronOCL
, to which we will pass the error gradient. Control is then passed to the
calcInputGradients
method of the parent class, but now with the
cNorm
object, which represents the normalized output of the attention module. This allows the gradient to be propagated correctly through the final stage of the forward pass.
The next key step is to call the
AttentNormGrad
method, which implements the support functions for the OpenCL program's kernel of the same name. Here it is important to correctly account for the effects of all previously applied statistical transformations, as well as the attention weights, to ensure consistent error propagation.
if
(!AttentNormGrad(cTranspose.AsObject()))
return
false
;
After that, the
CalcHiddenGradients
method of the
cAttention
object is called, allowing the error to be propagated from the level of the probability weights of the
SoftMax
function to the attention coefficients. This is important because attention weights, being functions of several input variables, require special handling when calculating the gradient.
if
(!cAttention.CalcHiddenGradients(cSoftMax.AsObject()))
return
false
;
if
(!MatMulGrad(NeuronOCL.getOutput(), PrevOutput,
                  cTranspose.getOutput(), cTranspose.getPrevOutput(),
                  cAttention.getGradient(),
                  iWindow, iCount, iWindow,
1
,
false
))
return
false
;
Next, the
MatMulGrad
function is called, which performs the backward operation for the matrix multiplication applied in the forward pass. Here, the input data and its transposed copy are taken into account. This makes it possible to reconstruct the gradients while preserving the internal relationships between the elements of the analyzed window.
However, it should be noted here that, at the transposed data level, we have already obtained the error gradient along the main branch of the data normalization flow. In addition, we still need to pass the data from the transposition object to the input data level. Therefore, at this stage, we store the obtained error gradients in auxiliary data buffers.
In the next step, we sum the error gradients obtained from the two information flows at the transposition object level.
if
(!SumAndNormilize(cTranspose.getGradient(), cTranspose.getPrevOutput(), cTranspose.getGradient(),
                       iWindow,
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
We pass the resulting values to the input data level, where we likewise sum the values from the two information flows.
if
(!NeuronOCL.CalcHiddenGradients(cTranspose.AsObject()))
return
false
;
if
(!SumAndNormilize(NeuronOCL.getGradient(), getPrevOutput(), NeuronOCL.getGradient(),
                       iCount,
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
//---
if
(NeuronOCL.Activation() != None)
if
(!DeActivation(NeuronOCL.getOutput(), NeuronOCL.getGradient(),
                       NeuronOCL.getGradient(), NeuronOCL.Activation()))
return
false
;
//---
return
true
;
  }
Finally, if an activation function was applied to the input data, its derivative is called using the
DeActivation
method. This completes the gradient propagation chain, ensuring that the error signal passes fully backward through all transformation stages.
It is worth emphasizing here that the entire implemented algorithm for extracting the spatial component, taking into account attention and normalization, contains no
trainable parameters
in the usual sense — that is, it contains neither weights nor biases nor internal coefficients that require optimization via gradient descent. All calculations are based solely on the current values of the input data, sample statistics, and the
SoftMax
function, which generates the attention distribution.
That is precisely why the
updateInputWeights
method, which is responsible for updating the model's parameters after each pass, is not overridden in this case. Instead, the stub implementation inherited from the parent class is retained. This solution is consistent with the project's overall architecture: it does not increase the model's complexity, does not require additional computations, and emphasizes the auxiliary, structural nature of this layer within the context of the entire neural network system.
The complete code for this class and all of its methods can be found in the attachment. Its structure highlights the carefully considered architectural design, as well as its tight integration with previously implemented components, making the module easy to scale and reuse within more complex neural network architectures.
Polynomial Regression Module
The next component we need to implement is the polynomial regression module. The authors of the
SSCNN
framework significantly expanded the component's architecture by adding
multiplicative interactions
to the additive connections. This extension made it possible to implement more complex and expressive forms of interdependencies among the model's input components.
Why is this necessary? Financial time series very rarely follow strictly linear or simply additive patterns. In reality, we are dealing with an interplay of trends, cycles, seasonality, and noise, among which complex, nonlinear relationships often emerge. The classical polynomial regression model, even with a large number of degrees of freedom, often proves insufficiently flexible to accurately describe such effects.
To adequately capture second-order (and even higher-order) interactions, the input signal is processed in parallel via two paths:
an additive path
implemented via a convolutional layer, responsible for capturing linear and weakly nonlinear relationships among independently acting features;
a multiplicative path
represented by a block of convolutional layers. It is here that the concept
of context-dependent modulation
of features is implemented, making it possible to account for nonlinear combinations and the mutual amplification or attenuation of components.
In our implementation, we went a step further by incorporating
SwiGLU
activation into the multiplicative path — one of the modern and effective nonlinearities that helps increase a model’s trainable capacity without significantly increasing the number of parameters.
The
CNeuronPolynomialRegression

OpenCL
environment. It inherits its main interfaces from the base class
CNeuronBaseOCL
, which ensures compatibility with the rest of the framework without the need for adaptation. The design of this layer is based on the principles of composition: each internal block is responsible for a clearly defined task, and the interaction between them forms a complex yet flexible system for processing the input signal.

The class contains three key components: the
cProjection
projection block, based on the
SwiGLU
mechanism, acts as the first data transformer. It performs feature expansion, preparing the features for further processing. In addition, two convolutional layers are used to capture residual and multiplicative relationships. This distinction makes it possible to combine both additive and polynomial (second-order and higher-order) relationships between features, thereby expanding the model's expressive power without unduly complicating its structure.
The internal architecture of the class is organized such that all its components are declared as static members. This means that they are created once during initialization and do not require dynamic memory allocation or manual lifetime management. This approach ensures simplicity of design, reduces overhead, and eliminates the need to explicitly define a class constructor and destructor — these methods remain empty, which underscores the conciseness and self-contained nature of the structure.
The entire internal architecture is configured in the
Init
method, which effectively initializes the layer's computational graph.

Now that we've covered the initialization methods, let's move on to the
heart of the computations
— the forward pass in the
feedForward

bool

if
(!cProjection.FeedForward(NeuronOCL))
return

;
if
(!cConvolution.FeedForward(cProjection.AsObject()))
return
false
;
First, we delegate the processing of the input data to the projection module
cProjection
, passing it a pointer to the object of the preceding neural layer. If something goes wrong at this stage, the function will immediately return
false
.
If successful, the result of the
SwiGLU
transformation is passed to the convolution block
cConvolution

The same input data is then fed into the linear block
cResidual

if
(!cResidual.FeedForward(NeuronOCL))
return
false
;
if
(!SumAndNormilize(cConvolution.getOutput(), cResidual.getOutput(),

true
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
//---
return
true
;

Once all three components have successfully processed the data, their outputs are passed to the
SumAndNormilize
function, where the branches are added element by element and normalized by the window size. We store the resulting values in the external interface's result buffer. Thus, without a single unnecessary pause, each step flows smoothly into the next, ensuring the cohesive and reliable operation of the polynomial layer.
After a successful forward pass, backpropagation begins in the
calcInputGradients

if
(!NeuronOCL)
return
false
;
The validity of the pointer to the input data object is checked immediately. If it is empty, the function immediately returns
false
without taking any further action.
Next, gradients are backpropagated from the convolution block into the projection module.
if
(!cProjection.CalcHiddenGradients(cConvolution.AsObject()))
return
false
;
//---
if
(!NeuronOCL.CalcHiddenGradients(cProjection.AsObject()))
return
false
;
Without waiting for any pauses, the method accesses the input data object directly by calling the
CalcHiddenGradients
method, which allows the gradients to be propagated down to the appropriate level.
Once this part is complete, we move on to propagating the error gradient along the second information flow. First, however, we save the pointer to the current buffer in the temporary variable
temp
so as not to lose the accumulated values. To process the residual (
linear

CalcHiddenGradients

CBufferFloat* temp = NeuronOCL.getGradient();
if
(!NeuronOCL.SetGradient(NeuronOCL.getPrevOutput(),
false
) ||
      !NeuronOCL.CalcHiddenGradients(cResidual.AsObject()) ||

false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
) ||

false
))
return
false
;
//---
return
true
;

SetGradient

true

Now that the gradients have been collected and are ready to be applied, we smoothly move on to the weight update stage in the
updateInputWeights

cProjection

cConvolution

Finally, the
cResidual

updateInputWeights

true
and ensuring that all components of
CNeuronPolynomialRegression
are synchronously ready for the next training cycle.

Today we made a significant breakthrough: three key components of the
SSCNN
framework have been successfully developed. Now it is time to take a breather so that this new knowledge and these new observations can settle in our minds, like dew at dawn. After taking a break, we will move on to the next stage with a clear head and renewed energy.
In the next article, we will link all the modules into a single computational chain and put them through a true
field test
— we will run the algorithm on historical market data to evaluate its stability and accuracy. On this
real-world proving ground
, we will test how elegantly and effectively our solutions perform. And, of course, we will draw conclusions that will help make
SSCNN
even more reliable and high-performing.
Conclusion
The transition from a conceptual description of the
SSCNN
framework to its implementation demonstrated how important structured design and consistency are at all levels of developing models focused on the analysis of market time series. The framework's authors deliberately rejected scaling as a one-size-fits-all approach in favor of decomposition and modularity — a principle that allows the model to remain interpretable, adaptive, and robust even in the face of high levels of market noise.
The
CNeuronAttentNorm
architecture embodies our approach: it combines semantically rich attention and normalization mechanisms implemented on the
GPU
, taking into account segment context and the characteristics of financial signals. The approach to initializing, transferring, and synchronizing data between the
CPU
and the
GPU
was designed to avoid the typical bottlenecks associated with parallel computing in
OpenCL
.
Particular attention was paid to training the attention parameters, allowing the model to selectively focus on the most significant parts of the signal being analyzed. This is not merely an improvement in forecast accuracy, but also a step toward meaningful generalization, where every component of the model — from structural decomposition to normalization — works in harmony with the context.
In the next article, we will combine all the components into a single algorithm and conduct
a field test
on historical financial data. This will allow us to evaluate the robustness and accuracy of
SSCNN
under real-world conditions.
